objectives: Ask a clear question in the classroom.
Use the right question word for what you want to know.
Wait for your turn to speak.
Say when you do not understand a word.
Ask a teacher or grown-up for help politely.
Ask a question when you are not sure, instead of staying quiet.

sections.body:
A question is a sentence that asks for something you do not know yet. That is all. *Where is the pencil?* *What time is it?* *Why is the sky blue?*

Questions are how children learn. A small child asks a question, gets an answer, and knows one more thing about the world.

In a classroom, questions are welcome. A teacher asks questions because they want the class to think. Students ask questions because they want to understand. Both kinds are good.

But not every question gets a good answer. A question that is too long gets lost. A question that is too quiet never gets heard. A rude question gets a cold answer.

So there is a way to ask well. And it is simple: **be ready, be clear, be polite, and be brave.**

In this article you will learn the question words, the right moment to speak, and the words you use when you are stuck.
examples: Can I ask a question, please?
sections.heading: What a question is, and why it matters

sections.body:
A good question at the wrong time still gets lost. Here is how to catch the right moment.

**Raise your hand.** In most classrooms, a raised hand is a ticket. It says *I have something to say*. Keep your hand up until the teacher calls on you. Waving your arms does not help.

**Wait your turn.** Another child is asking now. Listen to the answer. Your question may get answered by it.

**Stand up if you need to.** Some classrooms in Vietnam ask children to stand when they speak. Standing makes your voice easier to hear.

**Ask one question at a time.** If you have three questions, ask the first one. Then ask the next. A teacher has many children and little time.

**Keep it short.** *How do you make rain?* is a fine question. A long story before the question makes people lose the thread.

And if the answer comes, listen to it. Then ask the next one. Good questioners keep going.
examples: May I ask a question, please?
Sorry, I have one more question.
Can you say that again, please?
sections.heading: Asking at the right moment

sections.body:
The question words are the little keys that open different doors. Each one asks for a different kind of answer.

**What** asks for a thing or an idea. *What is this?* *What does that word mean?* It is the most useful word of all.

**Who** asks for a person. *Who is your teacher?* *Who made this?*

**Where** asks for a place. *Where is my bag?* *Where do you live?*

**When** asks for a time. *When does the lesson start?* *When are you coming?*

**Why** asks for a reason. *Why do we have to wash our hands?* A why question is the hardest and the most interesting.

**How** asks for a way or a manner. *How do you say this in English?* *How do you get to school?*

And **Can I** is a special question. It does not ask for information. It asks for permission. *Can I go to the toilet?* *Can I borrow your ruler?*

Learn the six words and you can ask almost anything.
examples: Why is it so hot today?

sections.body:
A question goes wrong in a few usual ways. This is the way that works.

First, wait for a gap. Not while the teacher is writing and the room is noisy.

Then raise your hand and keep it up.

Next, when your turn comes, stand up and speak clearly. Say the whole question, from the first word to the last.

After that, listen to the answer. If it was not clear, ask once more. That is not rude. *Sorry, could you say that again?*

Then say thank you. *Thank you.* Two small words, and the teacher knows you listened.

Finally, write the answer down if you need to remember it. A question you asked once is worth very little if you forget it.
examples: Sorry, could you say that again?
I did not catch the last word.
sections.heading: How to ask a question in class
steps: Wait for a quiet gap in the lesson.
Raise your hand and keep it up.
Ask again if the answer was not clear.
Say thank you when you get the answer.

sections.body:
Sometimes the person who can help you is standing right in front of you. Here is how to ask them well.

**Use their name.** *Cô ơi, con có thể hỏi một câu không?* A name makes it a conversation, not a shout.

**Be polite.** Words like *please*, *may I* and *thank you* are small, but they matter. In Vietnamese classrooms, students often say *Dạ* and *Vâng*. These little words show respect.

**Say the question, not the complaint.** *I do not understand this part* is better than *This is too hard*. A teacher can help with the first one.

**Ask your teacher a quiet question when nobody else is talking.** It is kinder to everybody, and you will get a better answer.

**If you are really stuck, ask your friend first.** *How do you say this in English?* Sometimes a classmate knows the word you are missing. Then you can thank your teacher with the word in your hand.

Being brave with a question is a skill. It starts small, and it gets easier every single time.
examples: Miss Lan, may I ask a question, please?
I do not understand this part. Can you help me?
What does this word mean in English?
sections.heading: Asking a teacher or a grown-up

sections.body:
Many children feel shy about asking in class. Your hand does not want to go up. That feeling is normal and it gets better.

Start with a tiny question. *Where do I put my book?* *What time is it?* Small questions are easy, and easy questions are how brave habits begin.

Ask your friend instead of the whole class first. *What did the teacher say?*

Write your question on a piece of paper and hand it to the teacher. Some children find this easier than speaking.

And remember this: your teacher wants you to understand. A question is not a mistake. It is the sign that you are paying attention.

If a question feels too big today, save it for later. A question that waits for you is still a good question.
examples: I can ask you later, if that is okay.
sections.heading: When you are shy about asking

item.summary: A good question is a small key that opens a big door. After reading this you can ask a clear question in class, use the right question words, wait for your turn, and ask a teacher or grown-up for help politely.
